entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Saint Malo (also known as Maclou or Mac'h Low), a Welsh Christian monk, stands as a pivotal figure in the evangelization of Brittany during the 6th and early 7th centuries, establishing the diocese and town that bear his name. Born in Wales around 520 CE, he became one of the "Seven Founding Saints of Brittany," instrumental in the Celtic Christian migration and the establishment of a distinct Breton ecclesiastical identity amidst the decline of Roman influence and the rise of Frankish power. His significance lies in bridging the Insular Celtic Christian tradition with continental Gaul, propagating monasticism, and foundational urban development in a crucial maritime region.

Malo's early life saw him educated at Llancarfan Abbey under Saint Brendan the Navigator, with whom he reportedly embarked on a journey to the "Isle of the Blessed" (possibly the Canary Islands or a legendary locale). Around 550 CE, he migrated from Wales to Brittany, settling near Aleth (modern-day Saint-Servan, part of Saint-Malo) on the Rance estuary. Here, he founded a monastic community and became the first bishop of Aleth, later known as Saint-Malo. His ministry involved converting local pagan populations and organizing the nascent Christian communities, often navigating the complex socio-political landscape of post-Roman Armorica, which was then experiencing significant British (Welsh and Cornish) immigration. He consecrated the first cathedral in Aleth, establishing an institutional presence for the church.
